name: Red Sails Lettuce
variety: Red Sails; named looseleaf lettuce variety (1985 AAS winner)
summary: Red Sails is a named looseleaf lettuce variety recognized by All-America Selections for its crinkled bronze-red leaves and ornamental as well as edible value. Supplier harvest dates are estimates, not guarantees.

identity.short: Named looseleaf variety of Lactuca sativa
identity.guidance: All-America Selections identifies Red Sails as looseleaf lettuce and its 1985 edible-vegetable winner. The award profile describes savoyed, crinkled bronze-red leaves; it does not establish a modern disease-resistance rating or guaranteed performance in every climate.

growth.short: Crinkled, bronze-red loose leaves; ornamental and edible
growth.guidance: AAS describes Red Sails as a savoyed, crinkled leaf lettuce that can also be used as decorative edging. Johnny's lists it for baby-leaf and full-size harvest. These are variety/product descriptions, not a claim that it forms a tight romaine head.

cultivation.short: Cool-season lettuce; keep root-zone moisture even
cultivation.guidance: UMN Extension describes lettuce as a cool-season crop with shallow roots. Keep moisture reasonably even: a dry spell followed by renewed water and rapid growth can be associated with tipburn. UMN's outdoor calendar and field spacing are regional guidance, not indoor lamp, nutrient, or pod-spacing prescriptions.

care.short: Choose baby-leaf or full-size harvest; regrowth is not guaranteed
care.guidance: Johnny's describes baby-leaf harvest by cutting above the growing point and removing harvest debris to support regrowth quality; its full-size instructions are distinct. Treat repeat harvest as a possible method, not a promise that every cut plant regrows uniformly. No pruning or thinning rule unique to Red Sails is established here.

harvest.short: Supplier estimates about 30 days for baby leaf, 55 for full size
harvest.guidance: Johnny's lists approximately 30 days to baby leaf and 55 days to full size. These are supplier estimates, not guaranteed dates. Its baby-leaf guidance is to cut leaves about 1 inch above the growing point when roughly 3–4 inches long; full-size instructions describe cutting the plant at the base. Choose the harvest form before interpreting maturity.

problems.short: Heat can trigger bolting, bitterness, and the end of leaf harvest
problems.guidance: UMN reports that high temperatures and long days can trigger bolting in lettuce; leaves may become bitter and normal leafy growth stops. If margins brown after a dry spell and renewed growth, consider moisture-related tipburn before assuming disease or nutrient deficiency. Red Sails-specific heat tolerance and disease resistance are not established by these sources.

name: Parris Island Romaine
variety: Parris Island; named open-pollinated romaine variety
summary: Parris Island is an open-pollinated romaine variety used for baby leaf and full-size harvest. Johnny's describes upright, medium-green oval leaves and gives separate supplier estimates for baby-leaf and full-size harvest.

identity.short: Named open-pollinated romaine variety of Lactuca sativa
identity.guidance: Johnny's identifies Parris Island as Lactuca sativa, an annual, open-pollinated romaine variety. The page is a seed supplier's product record; it supports this variety's stated traits and instructions, not universal romaine characteristics.

growth.short: Upright romaine with medium-green oval leaves
growth.guidance: Johnny's describes an upright, medium-green oval leaf and positions Parris Island as a standard green romaine for baby leaf. Its product listing gives about 29 days to baby leaf and 56 to full size; these are supplier crop estimates, not guaranteed head dimensions or indoor timing.

cultivation.short: Cool-season romaine; field spacing depends on harvest form
cultivation.guidance: Johnny's recommends cool-weather conditions and gives different field spacing for romaine heads versus baby-leaf rows. Those soil-production distances are not Garden pod counts. UMN notes lettuce's shallow roots and regional sensitivity to heat and moisture swings; adapt the outdoor calendar locally and do not infer hydroponic settings from it.

care.short: Succession sowing is an optional way to stagger harvest
care.guidance: Johnny's suggests sowing every 2–3 weeks for a continuous supply in its production context. For a home setup, treat succession as optional rather than a required cycle; thin or space for the intended head or baby-leaf form, and do not map field distances to system positions.

harvest.short: Harvest baby leaf or a romaine head
harvest.guidance: Johnny's lists approximately 29 days for baby leaf and 56 days for full-size plants. For baby leaf it advises cutting leaves around 1 inch above the growing point at roughly 3–4 inches; for a head it advises cutting at the base. These are supplier estimates and instructions; local conditions affect timing, and the two harvest stages are not interchangeable.

problems.short: Bolting and tipburn are useful warning signs
problems.guidance: UMN Extension describes heat and long days as bolting triggers in lettuce; bolting ends normal leafy harvest and can make leaves bitter. Browning margins after a dry spell followed by renewed watering can indicate tipburn associated with rapid growth. Neither sign alone proves a disease or nutrient deficiency; Parris Island-specific resistance is not established here.

name: Red Mustard Greens
summary: Red mustard is represented at Brassica juncea species/type scope, not as a named cultivar. NC State and USU Extension describe a cool-season outdoor crop grown in sun or part shade with consistently moist, fertile soil; heat and moisture stress can hasten bolting or intensify flavor. Red-selection dimensions and hydroponic suitability remain unknown.

identity.short: Brassica juncea red-mustard leafy type; no named cultivar
identity.guidance: This identity represents red-leaved mustard greens at Brassica juncea crop/type scope, not a named cultivar. UMN Extension groups mustard greens with leafy Brassicas for early-season baby-leaf production; its guidance does not establish the exact color, size or performance of a specific red selection.

growth.short: Variable mustard foliage; lower leaves may be broad and lobed
growth.guidance: NC State describes Brassica juncea as highly variable: lower leaves may be larger, stalked, lobed or toothed, while upper leaves are narrower. This is species-level morphology; the record does not assign a particular red selection's exact leaf shape, dimensions, or disease response.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; sun to part shade and consistently moist soil
cultivation.guidance: NC State and USU Extension describe mustard as a cool-season crop for spring and fall, in full sun or part shade, with rich, well-drained soil kept consistently moist. NC State notes that shade can help baby greens in hot weather; heat and moisture stress can hasten bolting or produce stronger flavor. These are outdoor crop/species recommendations, not indoor-light tiers or hydroponic proof.

care.short: Avoid moisture swings and reduce weed competition
care.guidance: USU Extension reports that uneven moisture can toughen leaves, slow development and contribute to off-flavors; mustard also competes poorly with weeds. Keep the root zone evenly moist in soil and remove competing weeds without cultivating deeply enough to damage roots. This does not establish a fixed watering schedule or indoor-system rule.

pruning.short: Manage by harvest rather than ornamental shaping
pruning.guidance: Use clean harvest cuts rather than routine ornamental shaping. Remove damaged leaves when needed; this is a conservative adaptation to an edible-leaf crop, not a species-specific pruning schedule.

harvest.short: Cut tender leaves and allow regrowth when the plant remains active
harvest.guidance: UMN Extension describes mustard greens as a cut-and-come-again crop group. Harvest stage and regrowth depend on the plant and setting; do not promise repeated cuts for every red mustard selection.

problems.short: Flea beetles can leave small round holes in leaves
problems.guidance: UMN Extension describes flea beetles as a concern on brassicas; adults leave small round feeding holes, and mustard is named among trap-crop examples. Its Minnesota row-cover and rotation guidance is crop-group level, not evidence of Red Mustard cultivar resistance or a universal treatment prescription.

growthHabits.reason: Brassica juncea has variable leaf forms; a stable growth-habit classification is not assigned to this red mustard type.

evidence.note: NC State supports full sun to part shade for Brassica juncea; outdoor exposure only, not an indoor grow-light tier or system response.

name: Watercress
summary: Watercress (Nasturtium officinale) is a perennial aquatic leafy herb grown for its peppery leaves and shoots. It needs persistently wet or shallow-water conditions; container guidance does not establish compatibility with a closed-loop indoor hydroponic system.

identity.short: Watercress is resolved at Nasturtium officinale and Watercress type type scope
identity.guidance: Utah State Extension identifies watercress as the perennial Nasturtium officinale and distinguishes it from annual garden cress (Lepidium sativum) and biennial wintercress (Barbarea vulgaris). The common name 'cress' alone is not enough to transfer one species' cultivation advice to another.

growth.short: Perennial, water-loving plant with edible leaves and shoots
growth.guidance: USU describes watercress as a perennial naturally associated with running waterways; leaves and shoots are cultivated for food. Its flavor is strongest in cooler conditions and becomes less potent after flowering or as temperatures rise above 85°F, according to this regional Extension guidance.

cultivation.short: Keep the root zone saturated or in shallow moving water
cultivation.guidance: USU reports that watercress grows best in saturated, organically rich soil or in submerged/shallow moving water. It describes container culture with the pot kept wet in a water-filled saucer or bucket. These outdoor/container methods are evidence of water needs, not proof of a Garden hydroponic model's safety or performance.

care.short: Do not let container media dry; refresh standing water regularly
care.guidance: For its bucket method, USU advises maintaining 2–3 inches of water around the pot so the media stays wet and roots are submerged, and changing that water once or twice weekly. This is a source-specific outdoor container method, not a general recirculating-system schedule.

pruning.short: Manage by harvest, thinning, and visible crowding
pruning.guidance: USU's harvest method cuts the plant back to about 4 inches so it can regrow for a later harvest. Use this only as the described outdoor watercress method; it is not a promise of uniform regrowth in another environment.

harvest.short: Harvest leaves and young stems before flowering for stronger flavor
harvest.guidance: USU recommends harvesting leaves and young stems before flowering; it notes flavor is best during cooler spring/fall conditions and weakens as temperatures rise above 85°F. Its suggested cut-back to about 4 inches is an outdoor regrowth method, not a fixed harvest size for every setup.

problems.short: Watch for whiteflies, spider mites and snails; avoid wild harvest
problems.guidance: USU lists whiteflies, spider mites and snails among common watercress pests, with leaf undersides and stippling/scorching among signs described for the insects. It also discourages collecting wild watercress because pollution can cause illness. Confirm pest identification and local water safety before acting or harvesting.

thinning.short: USU outdoor transplant spacing is not system spacing
thinning.guidance: USU gives 8 inches between transplants for its outdoor garden instructions. That row/bed distance must not be treated as a hydroponic pod interval or container-system capacity.

name: Redbor Kale
summary: Redbor is an F1 kale selected for uniform, frilly deep purple-red leaves. Johnny's lists roughly 55 days from direct sowing and notes that cold weather enhances its color, curl and flavor. General kale care is useful, but those supplier figures are not guarantees for every seed lot or garden.

identity.short: Redbor (F1) is a kale selection of Brassica oleracea
identity.guidance: Johnny's identifies Redbor as an F1 hybrid kale within Brassica oleracea. Its Redbor page describes uniform plants and frilly purple-red foliage; this supplier-specific selection is not evidence for all kale or every Redbor seed lot.

growth.short: Uniform plants with frilly, deep purple-red leaves
growth.guidance: The product source characterizes Redbor as extremely uniform and similar to Winterbor except for its purple-red color. It does not give a mature plant height or spread, so dimensions remain unknown rather than inferred from generic kale.

cultivation.short: Cool-season crop; fertile, well-drained soil and steady moisture support leaf quality
cultivation.guidance: Johnny's general kale guide recommends fertile, well-drained soil rich in organic matter and consistent moisture, and describes favorable cool temperatures. This is crop-level outdoor guidance, not a Redbor-specific hydroponic recipe or indoor-light requirement.

care.short: Cool weather can intensify Redbor's color, curl and flavor
care.guidance: Johnny's notes stronger color, leaf curl and flavor in cold weather. Treat this as a supplier-reported cultivar characteristic, not a guarantee of a particular purple intensity or frost response in every location.

pruning.short: Remove damaged leaves; preserve the growing point and younger leaves
pruning.guidance: For leaf harvest, clip selected outer leaves cleanly and leave young central growth intact. This is a practical application of kale's documented repeated leaf harvest, not a Redbor-specific pruning technique.

harvest.short: Clip individual leaves; supplier maturity estimate is about 55 days from direct sowing
harvest.guidance: Johnny's lists 55 days to maturity from direct seeding for its Redbor product. Extension guidance describes harvesting kale leaves at different stages: take older leaves while leaving younger ones growing. Actual timing varies with weather, planting method and conditions.

problems.short: Scout for cabbage worms and loopers; protect young plants when pressure warrants
problems.guidance: Johnny's general kale guidance notes cabbage worms and loopers and describes row covers as exclusion. Its note that sold seed lots tested negative for black rot and black leg applies to supplier seed lots and is not a claim that the Redbor cultivar itself is disease resistant.

thinning.short: Use field spacing only for outdoor rows; indoor spacing remains unknown
thinning.guidance: Johnny's kale guide gives outdoor row and plant spacing for its crop production context. Those measurements are not converted to Garden pod counts or a universal indoor system layout; no Redbor-specific hydroponic spacing is established.

name: Georgia Collards
summary: A collard-type Brassica grown for its broad edible leaves, not a heading heart. Keep the established plant evenly moist and harvest older outer leaves while leaving the center active for continued growth; the catalog does not equate this identity with the specific Georgia Southern cultivar.

identity.short: Georgia Collards is kept at collard-type scope within Brassica oleracea
identity.guidance: UF/IFAS classifies collards as Brassica oleracea var. viridis and separately names Georgia Southern among cultivars. Because this catalog identity is Georgia Collards, not explicitly Georgia Southern, cultivar-specific leaf traits are not transferred to it.

cultivation.short: Keep the established leafy plant growing in evenly moist soil
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS describes collards as an outdoor, full-sun crop that does well with moist soil and organic matter. This is regional garden guidance, not a cultivar-specific feeding rate, indoor light tier, or hydroponic recipe.

growth.short: Broad-leaved, non-heading collard growth habit
growth.guidance: Collards are leafy Brassica plants rather than a tight-headed cabbage. The selected evidence supports the crop habit but does not establish mature height or spread for this catalog identity.

care.short: Inspect leaf undersides for caterpillars and sap-feeding pests
care.guidance: UF/IFAS lists leaf-feeding beetles, caterpillars including loopers and diamondback moths, aphids, whiteflies, and stink bugs on collards. Look for the insect and its feeding pattern before choosing an IPM response; no Georgia Collards-specific resistance is established.

harvest.short: Pick outer leaves and leave the growing center intact
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends removing older outer leaves so new growth can continue from the center. It gives young leaves of about 10–12 inches as a quality cue in its home-garden context; that is not a cultivar-specific size or a fixed harvest schedule. Leaves allowed to age may become tougher and woodier.

problems.short: Leaf-chewing pests and dry soil are actionable warning signs
problems.guidance: Inspect for visible caterpillar or beetle feeding and keep soil moisture adequate. The UF/IFAS seasonal calendar is Florida-specific; this profile does not turn it into a universal planting window or diagnosis for a particular cultivar.

name: Red Streaks Mizuna
summary: Red Streaked Mizuna is a supplier-listed leafy selection within the broader mizuna group. Harris Seeds describes deeply serrated leaves with the darkest red color at baby-leaf harvest and stronger color in cool conditions; the profile does not assign formal cultivar status or generalize those traits to all mizuna.

identity.short: Red Streaks is a supplier/type label within the broader mizuna group
identity.guidance: RHS describes mizuna as a Japanese leafy brassica and reports that varieties differ in leaf shape and color. Kew accepts Brassica rapa and synonymises the infra-specific name B. rapa var. nipposinica; USDA GRIN records subsp. nipposinica and cites the Mizuna Group. Harris Seeds sells a Red Streaked Mizuna product, which supports this supplier/type label but does not establish a formal cultivar or seed-lot taxonomy. One Oregon State figure caption uses B. juncea, while its guide otherwise places mizuna within B. rapa; the profile retains that source-level discrepancy.

cultivation.short: Cool conditions support leaf growth and the supplier-described red color
cultivation.guidance: RHS describes mizuna as a cool-season green that grows best in mild, damp weather and recommends maintaining moisture; containers may dry more quickly. Harris Seeds says the Red Streaked Mizuna listing develops its best color in cool growing temperatures. These sources support outdoor/container context and a supplier-scoped color response, not an indoor light tier or hydroponic prescription.

growth.short: Leafy rosette with finely divided, serrated leaves
growth.guidance: RHS describes mizuna generally as a loose rosette with serrated leaves and reports plants around 20 cm tall; Harris Seeds describes the Red Streaked Mizuna product as deeply serrated. The height remains a crop-level reference, not a measurement for this selection.

care.short: Prevent stress that hastens flowering
care.guidance: RHS notes that hot, dry conditions can cause poor growth or premature flowering; regular watering helps summer crops last longer, and a cooler lightly shaded site may help during warm weather. These are outdoor growing observations, not indoor light classifications.

harvest.short: Pick young leaves repeatedly, or harvest larger leaves for cooking
harvest.guidance: Harris Seeds says the Red Streaked Mizuna product is best harvested at baby-leaf stage for its darkest red color. RHS identifies mizuna generally as a cut-and-come-again salad crop; young leaves can be used raw and larger leaves cooked. The product listing gives no cultivar-verified harvest calendar, so no days-to-harvest or yield promise is assigned.

problems.short: Heat and dryness can trigger premature flowering
problems.guidance: RHS reports that hot, dry conditions can lead to poor growth and bolting in mizuna. If a flower stalk forms and flowering becomes difficult to stop, RHS suggests harvesting the plant while leaves remain palatable; this is general mizuna guidance, not a Red Streaks-specific response.

name: Mexican Tarragon
summary: Mexican tarragon is Tagetes lucida, a distinct marigold-family herb rather than French tarragon (Artemisia dracunculus). UF/IFAS describes an upright, semi-woody plant with aromatic edible leaves and yellow flowers, grown in full sun with occasional irrigation after establishment. Its Florida-specific freeze response is not a universal hardiness rating; exact cultivar size and hydroponic suitability remain unestablished.

identity.short: Accepted species Tagetes lucida; distinct from French tarragon
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Tagetes lucida Cav. as a species in Asteraceae. UF/IFAS uses Mexican tarragon for this species and explicitly contrasts it with French tarragon, Artemisia dracunculus. The common name does not make them the same botanical identity.

growth.short: Upright, semi-woody herb with narrow leaves and yellow flowers
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes bright-green narrow foliage, small golden-yellow flowers, and a semi-woody upright bush; its Florida article reports 2–3 ft height. Treat that size as the source's regional horticultural description, not a guarantee for every climate or unnamed seed line.

cultivation.short: Full sun outdoors; occasional irrigation after establishment
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends full sun and reports drought tolerance after establishment, with better growth under occasional irrigation. In Florida it is perennial; the source says cooler climates may treat it as an annual and that a hard freeze kills top growth before usual spring recovery. Do not generalize Florida year-round growth to colder climates.

care.short: Harvest conservatively so the plant retains enough foliage
care.guidance: UF/IFAS cautions against clipping too much from the plant. The profile therefore supports selective use, not a fixed pruning interval or amount; local frost exposure and recovery should be observed rather than inferred from Florida conditions.

pruning.short: No fixed pruning schedule established
pruning.guidance: The UF/IFAS guidance recommends avoiding excessive clipping but does not prescribe a pruning calendar or stem length. Remove only what is needed for use or damaged growth, and leave enough healthy foliage for continued growth; the exact regrowth response is not quantified.

harvest.short: Harvest flavorful leaves fresh; avoid excessive clipping
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS recommends fresh use of the leaves and advises against clipping too much. It notes that drying and high cooking heat reduce flavor, so add leaves near the end of hot dishes; freeze or store in vinegar for longer keeping. No universal regrowth interval is supplied.

flowering.short: Yellow flowers can be used as edible garnish
flowering.guidance: UF/IFAS describes small golden-yellow flowers and says they can brighten salads; it reports fall flowering in Florida. That flowering season is regional and is not a universal calendar for this identity.

uses.short: Use the leaves as an aromatic tarragon substitute
uses.guidance: UF/IFAS describes anise-like flavor with mint and cinnamon notes, use in drinks, teas and cooking, and flowers as salad garnish. It is a culinary substitute, not French tarragon botanically; individual flavor varies and is not a medical claim.

problems.short: Hard freezes can kill top growth; sensitivity is climate-dependent
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS reports that a hard freeze kills the plant to ground level in its Florida context, with usual spring recovery, and that it is used as an annual in cooler climates. Kew describes the species as perennial in subtropical biome context. These sources do not establish a universal cold-hardiness threshold.

name: Purple Basil
summary: Purple Basil represents purple-leaf forms of Ocimum basilicum, not one named cultivar. NC State Extension describes showy purple foliage forms as ornamental as well as edible, with container use documented; cultivar-specific size, flavor, and disease resistance remain unresolved for this broad identity.

identity.short: Purple-leaf horticultural type within Ocimum basilicum
identity.guidance: NC State Extension lists Purple Basil as a common name for Ocimum basilicum and describes showy purple-foliage cultivars. The catalog record represents that broad horticultural type, not a named cultivar such as Purple Ruffles, Dark Opal, or Rubin.

growth.short: Purple foliage varies among cultivars; ornamental forms are documented
growth.guidance: NC State Extension says sweet-basil cultivars with showy purple foliage are often used ornamentally and are suitable for containers. It names distinct examples including Dark Opal Purple, Purple Ruffles, and Rubin; their traits are not interchangeable and none is assigned to this unspecific Purple Basil record.

cultivation.short: Full sun and moist, well-drained soil in outdoor guidance
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension gives species-level sweet basil guidance for full sun and moist, well-drained soil. This supports outdoor crop context, not an artificial-light duration, hydroponic prescription, or purple-cultivar-specific optimum.

pruning.short: Pinch long stems and flower buds to encourage branching
pruning.guidance: NC State Extension recommends pinching long stem tips and flower buds to promote a branching, bushy form in sweet basil. The instruction is species/crop-level and not a rule about the exact timing or amount of pruning for every purple cultivar.

flowering.short: Flower buds are a management choice, not a diagnosis
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension includes flower-bud pinching in general sweet-basil pruning guidance. If flowers are retained, the specific bloom color and timing depend on the cultivar; this profile does not assign a color or flowering calendar to the unspecified purple type.

harvest.short: Aromatic leaves are edible; exact harvest timing is unresolved
harvest.guidance: NC State Extension identifies sweet-basil leaves as fragrant and edible. Its page points to a regional planting and harvest calendar, but no single timing is assigned here to an unidentified cultivar or growing system.

use.short: Culinary and ornamental uses are both documented at crop scope
use.guidance: NC State Extension describes edible basil leaves used in soups, stews, and other dishes, and notes ornamental/container value for showy purple-leaf cultivars. The specific flavor profile and best culinary use vary by named cultivar and are not resolved for this broad record.

problems.short: Basil pests and diseases are crop-level risks; resistance is cultivar-specific
problems.guidance: NC State Extension lists aphids and Japanese beetles as occasional insect problems and Fusarium wilt and basil downy mildew among diseases. It names resistant cultivars, but this generic Purple Basil identity is not one of those resolved named selections; do not infer resistance.

evidence.note: Species-level source says pinching basil tips promotes a bushy form; no particular purple cultivar is represented.

evidence.note: NC State Extension lists full sun for sweet basil; outdoor species-level guidance only.

name: Cinnamon Basil
summary: Cinnamon basil is an aromatic Ocimum basilicum type distinguished by cinnamon-like scent and purple-toned stems/flowers. Sources differ on mature dimensions and flower-color wording; this profile preserves those differences and does not turn one seed product's measurements into a universal type specification.

identity.short: Cinnamon basil type within Ocimum basilicum
identity.guidance: NC State Extension lists 'Cinnamon' as a sweet-basil cultivar; Park Seed also sells a product under that name. Gardenpedia retains this broader Cinnamon basil type identity rather than asserting it is genetically identical to one supplier's seed lot. Kew supports the accepted parent species only.

growth.short: Cinnamon aroma and purple-toned stems/flowers; dimensions vary by source
growth.guidance: NC State Extension describes the named 'Cinnamon' cultivar as having purple flowers and stems, a strong cinnamon fragrance, and a height of about 2–2.5 ft. Park Seed reports about 3 ft tall and wide for its own 'Cinnamon' product. These are source-specific outdoor descriptions, so mature dimensions remain unresolved for this broader type record.

cultivation.short: Full sun and consistently moist, well-drained soil in outdoor sources
cultivation.guidance: NC State Extension gives full sun and moist, well-drained soil for sweet basil generally. Park Seed repeats those conditions for its named 'Cinnamon' product. Neither source establishes hydroponic compatibility or an indoor light-hour requirement for this type.

pruning.short: Pinching can differ with culinary versus ornamental goals
pruning.guidance: Park Seed's instructions for its 'Cinnamon' product advise pinching the central stem and pruning later stems for culinary leaf production; when grown ornamentally, it advises retaining buds and branching stems. This is one supplier's cultivar-specific instruction, not a universal schedule for every cinnamon basil seed lot.

flowering.short: Flower descriptions vary slightly between references
flowering.guidance: NC State Extension describes purple flowers and stems; Park Seed describes deep-pink to purple blooms for its named product and says flowering can attract bees and butterflies. The sources agree on purple-toned flowering but differ in color detail; no universal bloom date is assigned.

harvest.short: For leaf production, harvest stems while retaining active nodes
harvest.guidance: Park Seed's product guide says to pinch flowering buds for culinary production and describes cutting stems back to the first or second leaf set. This detailed technique is kept at the scope of that supplier's 'Cinnamon' product; no weekly yield or fixed schedule is generalized to all systems.

use.short: Spicy-sweet aroma for culinary and ornamental use
use.guidance: Park Seed describes its 'Cinnamon' basil as a spicy-sweet aromatic herb used in baked goods, pasta, salads, jams, oils, and vinegars. These are examples attached to that product description; flavor and preference are not claimed to replace Genovese basil in every recipe.

problems.short: Common basil pests and diseases; no resistance assigned to this type
problems.guidance: NC State Extension lists aphids and Japanese beetles as occasional insect problems and Fusarium wilt and basil downy mildew among diseases affecting sweet basil. It identifies resistance in particular named cultivars, but no resistance evidence here is specific to the represented Cinnamon basil type.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: Wave 4 accepted no identity-specific hydroponic evidence for this crop/type.

evidence.note: Species-level basil guidance describes pinching to promote branching; no cultivar-specific habit measurement is assigned.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted into a universal Garden system position rule.

evidence.note: NC State Extension lists full sun for sweet basil; outdoor crop guidance only.

name: Anise
summary: Anise (Pimpinella anisum) is an upright annual herb in Apiaceae, grown for fragrant foliage and its seed-like fruits used as spice. Sources describe full sun and a slow early growth phase; reported mature size and harvest timing vary by source and growing context.

cultivation.short: Cooler growing conditions help limit premature flowering

care.short: Keep established plants watered in prolonged dry weather; support only if needed

harvest.short: Cut tight-budded shoots and continue picking side shoots

identity.short: Chioggia is an Italian heirloom variety of Beta vulgaris

growth.short: Slightly flattened, globe-shaped roots with red-orange skin and red-white rings

cultivation.short: Cool-season beet that tolerates some shade
cultivation.guidance: UW–Madison describes Chioggia as a cool-season beet that tolerates some shade and prefers loose, well-worked soil rich in organic matter. Keep moisture adequate while roots develop; this outdoor guidance does not establish indoor-light or hydroponic requirements.

care.short: Keep the root shoulder covered and weed shallowly around the shallow roots
care.guidance: The Extension article advises covering enlarging root shoulders with soil to reduce discoloration/corkiness and avoiding deep cultivation because beet roots are shallow. Keep enough moisture for tender roots; drought can contribute to stringy, tough texture.

pruning.short: Do not transplant or disturb the root; remove crowded seedlings by pinching

harvest.short: Harvest when the root reaches usable size; 50–60 days is a variety reference

problems.short: Few major problems are reported; leafminers may mark foliage and dry roots can turn tough
problems.guidance: UW–Madison says beets have few significant pest or disease problems; leafminer tunnels often do not affect roots, while soil pests may cause superficial root damage.
